--- title: "Reproducibility and transparent reporting" description: "Which random choice actually moves your result — measured — and the small set of habits that make an analysis someone else can re-run." order: 4 categories: [reproducibility, interpretation] --- ## Why this matters An analysis that cannot be re-run is not a method, it is an anecdote. That is the principled argument and everyone agrees with it, which is why it changes nobody's behaviour. The practical argument is sharper. Machine-learning pipelines contain several independent sources of randomness, they are not equally important, and if you do not know which one dominates you will spend your effort on the wrong one. This page measures them, and the answer is not the one the `set.seed()` habit implies. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Two experiments The same analysis — split the survey 75/25, fit a random forest, report the test RMSE and the three most important predictors — run sixteen times. First varying only the forest's internal randomness, then varying only the split. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() modelling <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() one_analysis <- function(split_seed, forest_seed) { set.seed(split_seed) split <- initial_split(modelling, prop = 0.75) held <- testing(split) set.seed(forest_seed) fitted <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe(abundance ~ ., data = training(split)) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())) |> add_model(rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = forest_seed) |> set_mode("regression")) |> fit(training(split)) baseline <- rmse_vec(held$abundance, predict(fitted, held)$.pred) set.seed(forest_seed + 1) importance <- map_dbl(setdiff(names(held), "abundance"), \(variable) { mean(map_dbl(1:20, \(i) { shuffled <- held shuffled[[variable]] <- sample(shuffled[[variable]]) rmse_vec(held$abundance, predict(fitted, shuffled)$.pred) - baseline })) }) names(importance) <- setdiff(names(held), "abundance") tibble(rmse = baseline, top_three = paste(names(sort(importance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:3], collapse = " > ")) } model_randomness <- map_dfr(1:8, \(s) one_analysis(split_seed = 100, forest_seed = s)) split_randomness <- map_dfr(1:8, \(s) one_analysis(split_seed = s, forest_seed = 1)) bind_rows( mutate(model_randomness, varying = "the forest's own randomness"), mutate(split_randomness, varying = "which rows land in the test set") ) |> summarise(`lowest RMSE` = round(min(rmse), 3), `highest RMSE` = round(max(rmse), 3), `RMSE range` = round(max(rmse) - min(rmse), 3), `distinct top-three orders` = n_distinct(top_three), .by = varying) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|varying | lowest RMSE| highest RMSE| RMSE range| distinct top-three orders| |:-------------------------------|-----------:|------------:|----------:|-------------------------:| |the forest's own randomness | 4.579| 4.595| 0.016| 3| |which rows land in the test set | 3.755| 5.255| 1.500| 6|
::: ::: The forest's own randomness is close to irrelevant: across eight seeds the RMSE moves by **0.016**. Which rows landed in the test set moves it by **1.50** — nearly a hundred times as much, and more than twice the entire spread between the best and worst model in [the previous page's comparison](black-box-or-not.qmd). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_rows(mutate(model_randomness, varying = "the forest's own\nrandomness"), mutate(split_randomness, varying = "which rows land in\nthe test set")) |> ggplot(aes(rmse, varying)) + geom_vline(xintercept = rmse_vec(modelling$abundance, rep(mean(modelling$abundance), nrow(modelling))), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") + geom_point(size = 2.6, alpha = 0.65, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "test RMSE", y = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Test RMSE from sixteen runs of the same analysis. Varying the forest's random seed (left) moves the answer by 0.016. Varying which rows are held out (right) moves it by 1.50. The dashed line is the mean-only baseline for scale.](reproducibility_files/figure-html/fig-seeds-1.png){#fig-seeds fig-alt='A strip plot with two rows of points on a shared horizontal RMSE axis from about 3.7 to 5.3. The upper row, labelled the forest\'s own randomness, is eight points piled almost exactly on top of each other near 4.58. The lower row, labelled which rows land in the test set, is eight points spread widely across the axis from 3.75 to 5.25. A dashed vertical line sits at 4.82.' width=1500} ::: ::: And the importance ranking is unstable under both. Eight runs that differ only in the forest's seed produced **three** different top-three orderings; eight runs that differ only in the split produced **six**. ## What follows from that **Seeding is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.** `set.seed()` makes your run repeatable by you. It does nothing about the fact that a different quarter of your stations would have given a different number. **Report a distribution, not a split.** This is §7's argument arriving from a new direction. A single 75/25 split gives you one draw from a spread of 1.5 RMSE; ten-fold cross-validation gives you a mean and a standard error over the same data. The reproducible thing to publish is the resampling estimate and its spread, and the seed is then about repeating the *procedure*, not about pinning the answer. **Importance rankings need repeating explicitly.** As [page 1](feature-importance.qmd) showed, the count of splits in which a variable beats a noise column is stable where the ranking is not. ## The mechanics Everything below is what this site itself does, and the details are in `.claude/workflow.md`. **Seed immediately before the random thing, in the same chunk.** A `set.seed()` at the top of a document is worthless the moment anyone runs a chunk out of order, and notebooks get run out of order. Every chunk that resamples, bootstraps, initialises or tunes carries its own seed on the line above. **Know which engine takes its own seed.** `ranger` has a `seed` argument that makes it reproducible independently of `num.threads`, which is worth checking rather than assuming. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictors <- model.matrix(abundance ~ . - 1, modelling) |> as.data.frame() predictors$abundance <- modelling$abundance map_dbl(c(1, 2, 4), \(threads) { set.seed(7) ranger::ranger(abundance ~ ., data = predictors, num.trees = 300, seed = 1, num.threads = threads)$prediction.error }) |> (\(x) tibble(threads = c(1, 2, 4), `out-of-bag MSE` = format(x, digits = 15)))() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| threads|out-of-bag MSE | |-------:|:----------------| | 1|18.7165661204235 | | 2|18.7165661204235 | | 4|18.7165661204235 |
::: ::: Identical to fifteen digits. Not every engine is; check yours once and write down the answer. **Pin the package versions.** `renv` records every package and version in `renv.lock`, and `renv::restore()` rebuilds that library. Without it, "I re-ran your code and got a different answer" is usually a package that changed its default two releases ago. Commit the lockfile in the same commit as the analysis that needs it. **Cache the computed results, not just the code.** This site commits `_freeze/`, so the numbers in every page are the ones that were checked, and a rebuild does not silently re-estimate them. A results cache is a record of what was actually run. **Document the path from raw to analysed.** This project keeps `data/coastal-survey-raw.csv` as it came off the ship and applies each cleaning decision in a named function, so the transformation from raw to clean is code rather than a description of code. Every decision §2 argued for is one line you can read. **Record the environment with the output.** `sessionInfo()` in an appendix costs nothing and answers most "why don't I get your numbers" questions immediately. ## A reporting checklist Enough to let a competent reader reproduce your result, or say precisely why they cannot. | | | | --- | --- | | **Data** | Source, date of extraction, how many rows, how many dropped and why | | **Cleaning** | Every filter and transformation, as code, not prose | | **Split** | The resampling scheme, why it suits the dependence structure (§6, §7) | | **Model** | Family, engine, package version, every hyperparameter — including the ones you left at default | | **Tuning** | The grid searched, and whether the search sat inside the resampling | | **Metric** | Which one, why it matches the objective (§7), and the no-skill baseline | | **Uncertainty** | Spread across folds, not a single number | | **Seeds** | Stated, and the code arranged so they are actually used | | **Environment** | Lockfile or `sessionInfo()` | | **Negative results** | What you tried that did not work — the most commonly omitted item and often the most useful | ## Where this breaks down **Reproducible is not correct.** Everything on this page makes your number repeatable. Nothing on it makes the number right. The depth effect in [page 2](partial-effects.qmd) reproduces perfectly and is still not identified by the survey design. **Seeds do not survive everything.** A new version of a package can change a default, a sampling routine, or the order in which random numbers are drawn, and your seeded code will then give a different answer with no error. That is what the lockfile is for, and it is why `renv::restore()` matters more than `set.seed()`. **Computational reproducibility is the easy half.** Re-running the same code on the same data is a solved problem. Getting the same *conclusion* from a new survey is the one that matters, and it depends on the sampling design, the transferability of the model (§6) and the size of the effect — none of which a lockfile addresses. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - **The split dominates.** Across eight runs, changing the forest's random seed moved the test RMSE by 0.016; changing which rows were held out moved it by **1.50**. - Variable-importance rankings are unstable under both: eight runs gave three different top-three orders from the model's seed alone, and six from the split. - So **report the resampling distribution**, not a single split's number. The seed makes your procedure repeatable; it does not make one draw representative. - Seed in the same chunk as the random operation; pin versions with `renv`; commit the computed results; keep raw-to-clean as code. - **Reproducible is not correct.** A wrong answer reproduces exactly as well as a right one. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace the single 75/25 split with `vfold_cv(v = 10)` and repeat the experiment over eight different fold seeds. How much smaller is the spread, and is it smaller than the gap between the models on the previous page? 2. Run `one_analysis()` twice with identical arguments in a fresh R session. Do you get bit-identical results? Now delete one `set.seed()` line and try again.
